content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued updated guidelines for the screening and treatment of cervical pre-cancer lesions to prevent cervical cancer. These guidelines emphasize the use of dual-stain cytology as a triage test for women who test positive for high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV). Dual-stain cytology is performed on liquid-based cytology (LBC) slides and detects the co-expression of two proteins, p16 and Ki-67, in the same cell. The presence of both proteins indicates a positive result, suggesting an increased risk of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or 3 (CIN 2/3), also known as high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions. Cervical cancer remains a significant global health issue, ranking as the fourth most common cancer among women worldwide in 2022, with approximately 662,000 new cases and 349,000 deaths. It is the most common cancer in women in 25 countries, many of which are in sub-Saharan Africa. However, cervical cancer can be eliminated as a public health problem through the WHO Cervical Cancer Elimination Initiative, which aims to scale up prevention, screening, and treatment efforts. In May 2018, WHO Director-General Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called for action to eliminate cervical cancer. This led to the launch of the Global Strategy to Accelerate the Elimination of Cervical Cancer in November 2020. The strategy includes three key targets to be achieved by 2030: 90% of girls fully vaccinated with the HPV vaccine by age 15, 70% of women screened with a high-performance test by ages 35 and 45, and 90% of women identified with cervical disease receiving treatment. To support these goals, WHO updated its 2013 guidelines for cervical cancer prevention, focusing on simplifying screening and treatment algorithms. The updated guidance is being developed in four phases. The current guideline addresses the use of dual-stain cytology as a triage test, completing the second phase of the update. This approach is part of the screen, triage, and treat strategy, where treatment decisions are based on a positive primary screening test followed by a positive triage test. The guideline development process involved a systematic review and meta-analysis of data from cross-sectional and longitudinal studies to evaluate the accuracy of dual-stain cytology as a triage test. The evidence was reviewed by the Guideline Development Group (GDG), which applied the GRADE methodology to formulate recommendations. The GDG also considered factors such as acceptability, feasibility, resource use, and equity in their decision-making. The WHO emphasizes that dual-stain cytology is a valuable tool for identifying women at higher risk of cervical pre-cancer and cancer, enabling timely and appropriate treatment. This guideline complements previous recommendations on HPV DNA and mRNA testing for cervical cancer prevention.
